data.title: Mužla-Čenkov – a new reconstruction of the hillfort
data.excerpt: A Slavic hillfort with a dominant guard and military role stood at Mužla-Čenkov on the bank of the Danube in the 9th and 10th centuries. A year after the first attempt, Hradiská.sk and Dwarf digital archeology have substantially improved the visualisation of the site as it may have looked at the end of the 9th century, and have added a virtual tour.

children.text: A Slavic hillfort extended over the site of Mužla-Čenkov in the 9th and 10th centuries; parts of it lie in what is today the locality of Vilmakert. It can be counted among the hillforts with a dominant guard and military role. The site lies directly on the bank of the Danube, on today's border with Hungary. Thanks to its favourable position it was already occupied in prehistory, but it acquired its greatest importance in the period of the existence of Great Moravia.
A year ago Hradiská.sk, in cooperation with Dwarf digital archeology, already attempted to create
an approximate picture of the hillfort
in the period of its heyday. Our basis was two monographs by the archaeologists who excavated the hillfort.

Over the course of the year the equipment, the software and above all Dwarf's experience in the field of 3D visualisation advanced so far that we decided on a fundamental improvement of the original visualisation. As in the previous case, we are seeking to give an approximate idea of how the Slavic hillfort at Mužla looked sometime at the end of the 9th century.
Besides the video, you can also make use of a virtual tour of the hillfort, in which you choose for yourself which part of the hillfort you want to visit:

The course of the fortification, its composition and the density of the houses follow fairly closely the evidence from the archaeologists that we had available. Besides the dwelling houses, the hillfort of course also contained countless farm buildings, storage pits, refuse pits and all manner of objects of everyday use and clutter, which made up the everyday reality of the hillfort. We modelled some of these additional features, but even so this cannot, of course, be an exact reconstruction of everything that stood on the hillfort.
